prompt: How does molecular orbital (MO) theory describe covalent bond formation?

choices.text: Atomic orbitals on different atoms combine mathematically to form molecular orbitals that belong to the whole molecule
A singly occupied orbital on each atom overlaps to hold the shared pair
choices.why: That is the valence bond description.

choices.text: Electrons are transferred from one atom to another
choices.why: That describes ionic bonding.

choices.text: Each atom's hybrid orbitals stay on that atom and point toward the other
choices.why: Hybrid orbitals belong to the valence bond picture. In MO theory, the molecular orbitals belong to the entire molecule.

explanation: MO theory describes covalent bond formation as a mathematical combination of atomic orbitals (wave functions) on different atoms to form molecular orbitals, so called because they belong to the entire molecule rather than to an individual atom.

prompt: When two hydrogen 1s atomic orbitals combine in MO theory, how many molecular orbitals form?
explanation: Two atomic orbitals combine in two ways, an additive way and a subtractive way, giving two molecular orbitals: a bonding MO and an antibonding MO.

prompt: What is the additive combination of two hydrogen 1s orbitals?

choices.text: A bonding MO, lower in energy than the 1s orbitals and roughly egg-shaped
An antibonding MO, higher in energy, with a node between the nuclei
choices.why: That is the subtractive combination.

choices.text: Two overlapping 1s orbitals that stay separate
choices.why: The additive combination is a single egg-shaped molecular orbital, not two overlapping atomic orbitals as in valence bond theory.

choices.text: An orbital with the same energy as the 1s orbitals
choices.why: The additive combination is lower in energy than the two 1s atomic orbitals.

explanation: The additive combination gives a molecular orbital that is lower in energy and roughly egg-shaped. Its electrons spend most of their time between the two nuclei, bonding the atoms together, so it is called a bonding MO.

prompt: What is the subtractive combination of two hydrogen 1s orbitals?

choices.text: An antibonding MO, higher in energy, with a node between the nuclei
A bonding MO, lower in energy and egg-shaped
choices.why: That is the additive combination.

choices.text: A π bonding MO
choices.why: π MOs come from sideways combination of p orbitals, not from 1s orbitals.

choices.text: An orbital with the same energy as the 1s orbitals
choices.why: The subtractive combination is higher in energy than the two 1s atomic orbitals.

explanation: The subtractive combination leads to a molecular orbital that is higher in energy and has a node between the nuclei. It is called an antibonding MO.

prompt: Why can't electrons in an antibonding MO contribute to bonding?

choices.text: There is a node between the nuclei, so they can't occupy the central region
They are too low in energy
choices.why: Antibonding MOs are higher in energy than the atomic orbitals they come from.

choices.text: They are paired with opposite spins
choices.why: Bonding electrons are paired too. The problem is the node between the nuclei.

choices.text: They belong to only one atom
choices.why: Antibonding MOs belong to the whole molecule; it is the node that keeps their electrons out of the bonding region.

explanation: Any electrons in an antibonding MO can't occupy the central region between the nuclei, where there is a node, and so can't contribute to bonding. The two nuclei therefore repel each other.

prompt: In a ground-state H2 molecule, which molecular orbitals hold electrons?

choices.text: Only the bonding MO, which holds both electrons
Only the antibonding MO
choices.why: The two electrons go into the lower-energy bonding MO.

choices.text: Both: one electron in each
choices.why: Both electrons go into the lower-energy bonding MO; the antibonding MO is empty.

choices.text: Neither: the electrons stay in the 1s atomic orbitals
choices.why: In the MO picture the 1s orbitals are combined into molecular orbitals, and the electrons occupy the bonding one.

explanation: In H2, the lower-energy bonding MO is filled and the higher-energy antibonding MO is unfilled.

prompt: How many electrons are in the bonding molecular orbital of a ground-state H2 molecule?
explanation: Each hydrogen atom brings one electron, and both go into the lower-energy bonding MO. The antibonding MO is empty.

prompt: In ethylene, which description fits the π bonding MO?

choices.text: It combines p lobes of the same algebraic sign and has no node between the nuclei
It combines p lobes of opposite sign and has a node between the nuclei
choices.why: That is the π antibonding MO.

choices.text: It comes from head-on combination of two s orbitals
choices.why: Head-on s combination gives σ MOs, as in H2; π MOs come from sideways p combination.

choices.text: It is the higher-energy, vacant π MO
choices.why: The π bonding MO is the lower-energy one, and it is filled.

explanation: The lower-energy π bonding MO has no node between the nuclei and results from combining p orbital lobes with the same algebraic sign. It is occupied.

prompt: In ethylene, which description fits the π antibonding MO?

choices.text: It combines p lobes of opposite algebraic sign, has a node between the nuclei, and is vacant
It combines lobes of the same sign and has no node
choices.why: That is the π bonding MO.

choices.text: It is the lower-energy, filled π MO
choices.why: The antibonding MO is higher in energy and empty.

choices.text: It comes from the sp2 hybrid orbitals
choices.why: The π MOs come from the unhybridized p orbitals.

explanation: The higher-energy π antibonding MO has a node between nuclei and results from combining lobes with opposite algebraic signs. Only the bonding MO is occupied; the antibonding MO is vacant.

prompt: How does the MO description of the H2 bond differ from the valence bond description?

choices.text: The bonding MO is one egg-shaped orbital of the whole molecule, not two overlapping 1s atomic orbitals
MO theory says H2 has no bond
choices.why: MO theory also describes a bond, through the filled bonding MO.

choices.text: MO theory uses sp3 hybrid orbitals for hydrogen
choices.why: Neither description uses hybrid orbitals for hydrogen; both start from the 1s orbitals.

choices.text: In MO theory the electrons stay on separate atoms
choices.why: In MO theory the electrons occupy molecular orbitals that belong to the whole molecule.

explanation: The additive combination is a single, egg-shaped molecular orbital; it is not the same as the two overlapping 1s atomic orbitals of the valence bond description.

prompt: What shape is the antibonding MO of H2?

choices.text: An elongated dumbbell
A sphere
choices.why: Spheres are s atomic orbitals; the antibonding MO has a node between the nuclei.

choices.text: An egg shape
choices.why: That is the bonding MO.

choices.text: A cloverleaf
choices.why: Cloverleaf shapes belong to d atomic orbitals.

explanation: The subtractive combination is a single molecular orbital with the shape of an elongated dumbbell and a node between the nuclei.

prompt: When the two p orbitals of the C–C π bond in ethylene combine, how many π molecular orbitals form?
explanation: As with the σ MOs of H2, two atomic orbitals combine in two ways: a lower-energy π bonding MO and a higher-energy π antibonding MO.

prompt: Which of ethylene's two π molecular orbitals is occupied?

choices.text: Only the bonding MO
Only the antibonding MO
choices.why: Electrons fill the lower-energy bonding MO.

choices.text: Both, with one electron each
choices.why: The two π electrons pair up in the bonding MO; the antibonding MO is vacant.

choices.text: Neither
choices.why: The two π electrons occupy the π bonding MO.

explanation: Only the π bonding MO is occupied; the higher-energy, antibonding MO is vacant.

prompt: For what kind of compound is molecular orbital theory said to be particularly useful?

choices.text: Compounds with more than one double bond, for describing their π bonds
Ionic compounds like sodium chloride
choices.why: MO theory describes covalent bonds; the book points to π bonds in compounds with several double bonds.

choices.text: Simple alkanes like ethane
choices.why: Single-bonded alkanes are well described by valence bond theory and hybrid orbitals.

choices.text: Single atoms
choices.why: MO theory describes molecules, as the name says.

explanation: Molecular orbital theory is particularly useful for describing π bonds in compounds that have more than one double bond; the book returns to it in Chapters 14, 15 and 30.

prompt: How many nodes lie between the nuclei in the σ antibonding MO of H2?
explanation: The subtractive combination has one node between the nuclei, which is why electrons in it can't help hold the atoms together. The bonding MO has none.
